title: Free fermion models with an operator entanglement growing as $O(\sqrt{t})$
abstract: We study the time evolution of the Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE) of one-dimensional number-conserving free fermions subject to a random space- and time-dependent evolution. It is known that, in free-fermion systems without randomness, the OSEE of \emph{local} operators grows at most \emph{logarithmically} in time. Here we show that, in the presence of randomness, the OSEE of local spin operators involving a Jordan-Wigner string grows as $\mathcal O(\sqrt t)$, for all values of the Rényi index. We establish this in two models: a Brownian Hamiltonian and a brick-wall matchgate circuit. We also consider the OSEE of the evolution operator, and we show that it also grows as $\mathcal O(\sqrt{t})$, in contrast with the linear growth generically expected without randomness. We analytically compute the average entropies of the two operators by mapping the quantum models to the symmetric simple exclusion process, relying on an assumption of self-averaging which we support numerically. We also consider two other types of randomness: random evolution in time that keeps spatial translation invariance, and quenched disorder. In the former case, we find that the OSEE also grows as $\sqrt{t}$. In the latter case, we find that the entropy grows as $\mathcal O( \log \log t)$ for Hamiltonian evolution both for local operators with a Jordan-Wigner string and for the evolution operator, whereas it remains bounded at all times in the brick-wall matchgate circuit.
summary: This work analyzes how randomness affects the Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE) in 1D free fermion systems. The key finding is that disorder drives the OSEE to grow as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{t})$, a significant departure from the logarithmic growth expected in clean systems. The methodology involves mapping the quantum dynamics to solvable statistical models like the SSSEP.
main_problem: The study investigates the time evolution of the Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE) for local operators in 1D free fermions subjected to random space- and time-dependent evolution.
main_result: In the presence of randomness, the OSEE of local spin operators involving a Jordan-Wigner string grows as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{t})$, contrasting with the logarithmic growth seen in clean systems.
method: The authors analytically compute average entropies by mapping the quantum models to the symmetric simple exclusion process (SSSEP) and utilize vectorization techniques for Gaussian operators.
model_or_system: The system is one-dimensional number-conserving free fermions, modeled using specific Hamiltonians like the Brownian Hamiltonian or a brick-wall matchgate circuit, and analyzed under various types of randomness (spatio-temporal disorder, quenched disorder).
key_observables: Operator Space Entanglement Entropy (OSEE), $S_\alpha^A(O)$, for local operators and the evolution operator $U(t)$.
important_parameters: The Rényi index $\alpha$, and the time $t$ (showing $\sqrt{t}$ or $\log \log t$ scaling).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on an assumption of self-averaging, which is numerically supported, and the use of the Jordan-Wigner string operator as a key diagnostic.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares OSEE growth under fully random spatio-temporal disorder for the JW string and evolution operator. Figure 9 shows OSEE for the JW string under temporal disorder and translational invariance, comparing results to theoretical predictions.
paper_structure:
The paper first establishes the baseline for clean systems (logarithmic growth) before introducing randomness. It then analyzes specific random models (Brownian Hamiltonian, matchgate circuit) to derive the $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{t})$ scaling. Finally, it contrasts this with other disorder types (quenched disorder) and examines the special case of momentum conservation ($
u=1$).
why_interesting: The $\sqrt{t}$ scaling of entanglement entropy in disordered free fermion systems provides a quantitative measure of how randomness fundamentally alters quantum information spreading compared to integrable or clean systems.
